terms.comment: Properly ‘doing no harm’, in- and nocēns (Cic. Tusc. 5.41); of the accused, not guilty. Of what, in the genitive (Tac. Ann. 4.34, Lewis & Short).
Not in Cicero or Caesar; Plautus, Sallust, Livy and the poets (Lewis & Short).
Of a charge, with dē and the ablative, more rarely the genitive (Traupman 193).

phrases.latin: haec propter illōs scrīpta est hominēs fābula quī fictīs causīs innocentēs opprimunt
phrases.english: this fable was written for those people who crush the innocent with made-up charges

phrases.latin: innocēns is dīcitur, nōn quī leviter nocet, sed quī nihil nocet
phrases.english: a man is called innocent not if he does little harm, but if he does none
